newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian oil refineries sees privatisation distant.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian oil refineries sees privatisation distant.

text.p: Nigeria's ailing oil refineries see privatisation some way off and are hoping for more government money and better returns in 1997, the managing director of the largest refinery said.

"Eventually I expect they will be privatised in line with the global trend, but I don't see it happening next year," Mansur Ahmed, managing director of the Port Harcourt refinery told Reuters in Abuja.
"Nobody here has enough money to run the refineries, and why should anyone outside want to buy them when even in other parts of the world refineries are closing down."
Although Nigeria is among the world's 10 biggest oil producing nations it has often been forced to import fuel to cover local shortages.
Like the rest of the state sector the four oil refineries are victims of years of mismanagement and neglect.
They currently manage to process about 250,000 barrels per day (bpd) from a theoretical capacity of 445,000 bpd
The military government says the refineries will eventually be privatised, once their value has been determined and a formula found for selling them off.
Bids were invited in October from oil companies who might be interested in taking an interest in the refineries.
But NNPC sources said the bids that had been received so far were for management rather than purchase and might cost the government more to run than the present system.
Ahmed said the refineries hope to receive about $250 million from the government in 1997 to be able to carry out necessary repairs and maintenance.

"What we really need to bring the refineries up to capacity is $800 million, but I don't see that coming and with the lower amount we could expect to process up to 320,000 barrels per day by the end of the year," he said.
Ahmed estimated Nigeria's need at 280,000 bpd.
The refineries are also looking for an improvement in the government fixed pricing structure which allows refineries less than they need.

Currently the margin allocated to the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC) for both refining and distribution is 1.7 naira ($0.021) per litre from a pump price of 11 naira ($0.138) per litre.
"In theory it means we get around 72 cents a barrel for refining, but in practice we get as little as 40 cents a barrel," said Ahmed.
"We need an increase in our own margin to at least 5.0 naira ($0.063) a litre."

Receiving 5.32 naira ($0.066) per litre the biggest beneficiary of petrol sales in Nigeria is the Petroleum Trust Fund, set up to cushion the blow of a four-fold price increase in 1994 through spending on the economy.
The World Bank has long been pushing the military government to lift its effective fuel subsidy and allow prices to reach market levels.
Industry analysts say that if properly run, Nigeria's refineries are some of the few on the continent that could be potentially profitable, if they were to supply the West and Central African region.
($1=80 naira)
